fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says the people of Judah and Israel were "…eating and drinking and rejoicing." (1 Kings 4:20) They were as numerous as the sand on the seashore, so that's a whole lot of rejoicing. That's a party with a guest list I could never bake for.

Not quite, friend. Look at what the text says: the people of Judah and Israel "…were eating and drinking and rejoicing." (1 Kings 4:20) That's a whole crowd, as numerous as the sand on the seashore. Rejoicing is what the verse names, so True is the one it backs up.

Not what the text says, friend. It says these kingdoms "…offered tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life." (1 Kings 4:21) That verse describes tribute and service, not rebelling. Rebelling every chance they get isn't in it.

That's right, friend. The text says the kingdoms "…offered tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life." (1 Kings 4:21) Offering tribute and serving is what the verse describes, so rebelling every chance they get doesn't match. I would LOVE for my dough to cooperate like that.

Yes, friend! The text says Solomon "…had peace on all sides." (1 Kings 4:24) He had dominion over all the kingdoms from Tiphsah to Gaza, and peace came with it. Peace on all sides, no matter which way he turned.

I see why you'd think that when a king rules so much land, friend. But the text says Solomon "…had peace on all sides." (1 Kings 4:24) Enemies aren't what the verse names. It names peace, in every direction.

Good thought, friend, since David was Solomon's father (1 Kings 2:12). But the text says "…God gave Solomon wisdom, exceedingly deep insight, and understanding beyond measure…" (1 Kings 4:29) The giver is God. David isn't named as the one who gave it.

I can see why Nathan comes to mind, friend. His name shows up in this passage as the father of two of Solomon's officials (1 Kings 4:5). But the text says "…God gave Solomon wisdom, exceedingly deep insight, and understanding beyond measure…" (1 Kings 4:29) God is the giver, plain and simple.

Right you are, friend. The text says "…his fame spread throughout the surrounding nations." (1 Kings 4:31) Solomon's name got out past the border and into other nations. I was famous in exactly one junk drawer, so I'm taking notes.

Sounds like a smart move, friend, but the text doesn't mention a library. It says "Solomon composed three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered a thousand and five." (1 Kings 4:32) Proverbs and songs are what it names. I can't even keep my recipe box in order, so a library would be way over my head.

I get the idea, friend, since kings did hear about him. But this verse doesn't mention letters. It says "Solomon composed three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered a thousand and five." (1 Kings 4:32) What the passage says about the kings is that they sent men to listen to him (1 Kings 4:34).

That's right, friend. The text says "…he taught about animals, birds, reptiles, and fish." (1 Kings 4:33) He spoke of trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop growing in the wall, and then taught about those creatures too. Trees, animals, birds, reptiles and fish, all in one man's teaching.

You got it, friend. The text says "…men of all nations came to listen to Solomon’s wisdom, sent by all the kings of the earth, who had heard of his wisdom." (1 Kings 4:34) Kings sent their own people just to listen. That's a king saying, go sit in on that teaching for me.
